paras: The attempted lynching of Tom Hayes was a failed attempt by a mob to take Tom Hayes (also spelled Hays), a Black man accused of murder, from the jail at Andalusia, Covington County, Alabama, on the night of August 24–25, 1910. According to Sheriff W. T. Prestwood, a mob gathered a few miles from town, but its advance party turned back after finding the jail guarded by the local militia company. Hayes was taken the next morning to the Montgomery County jail, where he had been held after a crowd pursued him at his arrest in July. The Montgomery Advertiser, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Pensacola Journal each reported the episode as a narrow escape from lynching.

Hayes was accused of killing R. D. Sowell, a white night watchman at the Empire Lumber Company's yard about a mile from Andalusia, on the night of July 30–31, 1910. The Pensacola Journal called Hayes a "blind tiger" negro against whom Sowell had been a witness for selling whiskey; the Advertiser said the motive was not known.

When the body was found on July 31, mill workers set out after Hayes, and Deputy Sheriff J. M. Johnson raced him by automobile to the station at Gantt ahead of a crowd that, the Advertiser said, "seemed bent upon lynching." From Gantt he was taken by train to the Montgomery County jail, where, according to the Advertiser, he said he had not killed Sowell. Montgomery Sheriff Horace Hood later said that prisoners had seen Hayes washing a bloody undershirt and that Hayes had confessed to him, a claim the Age-Herald called an "alleged confession."

On Monday, August 22, Prestwood took Hayes back to Covington County for trial. The Advertiser reported that no further lynching attempt was expected locally, but the Age-Herald wrote that "the belief was general" that Hayes would be lynched, and an Associated Press dispatch gave him "not more than half a chance" of escaping a mob.

According to the Advertiser, Prestwood heard on Tuesday night, August 23, that a mob would storm the jail and had the militia held in readiness, but nothing happened. On Wednesday night he was told that a mob, which the Advertiser put at 250 men, had organized several miles from town and planned to storm the jail at 2 a.m. Accounts differ on the hour he learned of it: the Associated Press gave about 2 a.m., the Age-Herald "about 2 p. m."

After runners he sent out confirmed the report, Prestwood called out the militia company, and soldiers surrounded the jail. Some hours later an advance party of about 25 men (25 or 30, per the Advertiser) came into Andalusia, "evidently to reconnoiter." Finding the jail guarded, the men left, and nothing more was heard of the mob. On the morning of Thursday, August 25, Prestwood took Hayes to Montgomery on the first train out of Andalusia.

The Advertiser expected Hayes to be kept in Montgomery until his trial, and the Age-Herald reported that feeling remained high and that he would likely be killed if taken back. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage through September 1910.

The Montgomery Advertiser, published where Hayes was jailed, gave the fullest account under the headline "Sheriff Foils Plans of Mob," describing the scouting party facing a "line of steel." The Pensacola Journal ran the Associated Press version on its front page under "Narrow Escape From Lynching at Andalusia," after an August 22 dispatch headed "Take Negro to Danger Zone." The Birmingham Age-Herald's Montgomery correspondent headed his story "Negro Narrowly Escapes Violence" and wrote that Hayes had returned to "the bad boarders of Sheriff Horace Hood with a sigh of relief."

The papers credited the sheriff and the soldiers with saving the prisoner and named no member of the mob. At the same time they treated the murder charge largely as settled, calling it a "brutal murder," detailing the throat-cutting and repeating the confession attributed to Hayes, with the Age-Herald stating flatly that "Hayes killed a white man." No Black newspaper account of the episode appears in the coverage.
Only the Advertiser gave the mob's total size, 250; the wire and Age-Herald reports numbered only the advance party of about 25.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Tom Hayes
bases: A mob reportedly organized to storm the Andalusia jail and lynch a Black prisoner accused of murder, and turned back when it found soldiers guarding the jail (A7, A8, A9).

No one was killed: the mob's advance party found the jail guarded and withdrew, and Hayes was taken to Montgomery (A7, A8, A9); this was an attempted lynching by a group of 25 to 250 acting on a murder accusation (A7, A8).

The Montgomery Advertiser, an Associated Press dispatch and the Birmingham Age-Herald's correspondent agree on the mob forming, the militia guard, the scouting party's retreat and Hayes's removal, though all rest on Sheriff Prestwood's statements (A7, A8, A9).

accounts.label: Sheriff Prestwood (via the Montgomery Advertiser)
accounts.gist: After a false alarm Tuesday, he learned Wednesday night that 250 men had organized to storm the jail at 2 a.m.; he called out the militia, and 25 or 30 scouts came, found the jail protected and left.

accounts.label: Wire report (Associated Press)
accounts.gist: Hays escaped lynching only because soldiers guarded the jail; a mob was forming a few miles out and its 25-strong advance guard found the jail too well protected.

accounts.label: Age-Herald Montgomery correspondent
accounts.gist: Sheriff's runners confirmed a mob forming; about 25 men rode up, saw the guard and went back; feeling was high and Hayes would likely be killed if returned.

accounts.label: Sheriff Hood's account of a confession
accounts.gist: Prisoners saw Hayes washing a bloody undershirt and he later confessed to cutting Sowell's throat; Hayes had earlier told the jail he did not kill Sowell.

framing.detail: The Montgomery Advertiser's headline 'Sheriff Foils Plans of Mob' credited the sheriff and the 'line of steel', while calling the killing a 'brutal murder' and repeating the confession as 'said to have'.
The Pensacola Journal ran the AP story on page one, 'Tom Hays Taken Back to Montgomery After Narrow Escape From Lynching at Andalusia', after an Aug. 22 dispatch headed 'Take Negro to Danger Zone'.

The Birmingham Age-Herald headed it 'Negro Narrowly Escapes Violence', stated flatly that 'Hayes killed a white man', and joked that he returned to 'the bad boarders of Sheriff Horace Hood with a sigh of relief'.
